comparisons.basis: The complete Orate invitation and response dialogue in each identified edition share the invitation to pray for acceptance of the sacrifice. This is alignment of the same liturgical function, not a claim that the two response compositions are identical.

comparisons.apparatus_caveat: Only the selected collect entries have been transcribed and independently checked, not the entire formularies or books. Each is one continuous priestly block. Printed shortened conclusions Per. and Per Dominum nostrum. are retained without supplying a doxology. Abbreviations, long s, u/v, ae ligatures and line layout are normalized as declared in the artifacts. The separate retained pages establish the changed Gospel and Sunday heading; those observations are not represented as full Gospel transcriptions. Printing dates do not date the introduction of the changes; intervening editions and immediate ancestry remain unestablished.
comparisons.basis: The complete printed collect entries in two Suscepimus Deus formularies perform the same liturgical function but are different compositions: Deus cuius providentia in 1550 and Largire nobis in 1604. The named formulary supplies the pairing anchor. The earlier heading is Dominica octava after Trinity; the later heading is Dominica sexta after the octave of Trinity. No identical numbered Sunday is assumed.

comparisons.apparatus_caveat: This is one dated calendar cell, not a claim that Teresa is absent from every part of the 1574 missal or that the whole calendar has been collated. Other computistical columns are omitted. The 1621 printed date remains October 5 and is not modernized to October 15. Abbreviations, ampersands and the cōm. macron are preserved; e-caudata/ligature and long s are normalized as declared. The printed common-Mass reference at p.409 is separately retained, with manuscript alterations excluded. Exact introduction date, chapter intervention and immediate textual ancestry remain unestablished.
comparisons.basis: The same bounded printed October 5 calendar row is compared in two Carmelite missals. In 1574 the date numeral is present and its feast cell is empty; the normalized body is therefore only 5. In 1621 the cell names Teresa, duplex minus, with Placidus and companions commemorated and page reference 409. Calendar entries are explicitly typed as calendar rows, not spoken prayers.

comparisons.apparatus_caveat: The transcriptions preserve edition-specific e/ae and presbiter/presbyter, with abbreviation expansion, long-s, u/v, i/j, case, punctuation, accents and line layout treated as declared in each artifact. Lexical agreement under those declared normalizations does not establish substantive prayer revision. The 1804 title identifies a new printing of the Cisneros book, but does not identify the immediate exemplar of this blessing. Neither bibliographic succession nor changed printed placement establishes direct 1500-to-1804 textual parentage or the date of relocation. No Git parent, inheritance, complete Ordinary or whole missal is claimed.
comparisons.basis: Both identified printings carry the complete source-defined Benedictio panis, with the same heading, opening dialogue, Benedic Domine prayer, blessing and final sprinkling rubric. All nine ordered semantic units are independently collated. In the 1500 witness the blessing follows the final index and precedes the colophon; in 1804 it appears among preliminary blessings on p. XVI. The comparison aligns the complete blessing constituents, not the surrounding books.

source_record.note: Brightman printed lxx lists a 1288 witness containing Basil, Gregory and Cyril. The BCEP autoptic record gives the colophon date Amshir AM 1004 (1288, f. 131v), production at the Monastery of St Antony, contents (pre-anaphora ff. 2r–32r, Basil ff. 32v–65r, Gregory ff. 66r–103r, Cyril ff. 104r–125r, occasional prayers and the filling of the chalice), a later binding with Roman Catholic arms and the Latin spine title 'Liturgia Copta', and Latin marginal directions at the institution narrative in Gregory (ff. 81r–v). The complete offered image sequence (133 openings) was acquired in research scratch. Image 0133 shows the Arabic colophon (f. 131v), dated Amshir of the year 1004 of the Martyrs and naming the scribe Butrus, as the BCEP record reports; image 0082 (ff. 80v–81r) shows the Latin note beside the bread words. Later Latin notes and binding show Western readers or owners, not Catholic liturgical reception. No identification as Tuki's direct exemplar.

source_record.note: Original acquired from ULB Bonn (Goussen 1665). Propaganda Fide pro negotiis Ritus Orientalis approved the book on 25 February 1913 as revised and purged of errors, for priests of the rite received in Abyssinia; the Vicar Apostolic of Eritrea, C. Carrara, gave the imprimatur at Asmara on 12 April 1913. The title-page imprint reads ፲፱፻፯, equated with 1914/15 by Hammerschmidt and the Encyclopaedia Aethiopica. Section headings show the Apostles anaphora, an order of Communion and anaphoras numbered 2 to 14 (Our Lord; Mary; John son of Thunder; 318 Orthodox; Athanasius; Basil; Gregory of Nyssa; Epiphanius; John Chrysostom; Cyril; Dionysius; a heading for Däbrä Zäyt and Ṗagʷəmen; Gregory of Armenia), consistent with the Keren studies' count of fourteen. The New Catholic Encyclopedia reports Carrara sought to reprint the 1890 missal; the approbation's wording claims revision, so whole-book identity with 1890 is not established. Bonn's catalogue calls it a second edition and quotes a Keren 1890 imprint phrase not found on the pages inspected. Stable ID retained.

source_record.church_scope: Ethiopian Catholic liturgical history; later Eritrean reception chronology requires separate proof
source_record.limitations: Exact title, holding copy, decree and page loci remain missing. No claim that 2025 retains these changes.
source_record.note: Seventeen-anaphora Catholic edition. Bishop Kidane Yebio identifies it as the source of a literal Blin translation, establishing bounded Eritrean reception. A Keren 2009 Tigrinya study compares a specific Spirit invocation across 1890, 1913 and 1945 and lists three added anaphoras; the table does not mean earlier books lacked every epiclesis. The publisher’s signed 2024 note explicitly says the new edition replaces 1945. Exact original 1945 pages and editorial decree remain unacquired. The Encyclopaedia Aethiopica (mirror) says the Vatican press prepared it under Arnold van Lantschoot to correct earlier editions and lists 17 anaphoras: Apostles, Our Lord, Mary I, Mary II, John the Evangelist, James the Lord's brother, Mark, 318 Orthodox, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Epiphanius, John Chrysostom, Cyril, Jacob of Serug, Gregory and Dioscorus; it adds that the book's index (p. 7) does not name the last explicitly as Dioscorus of Alexandria but calls it the anaphora with which the missal ends. The Enciclopedia Cattolica (vol. VII, 1951, 'Libri liturgici', third-party transcription) instead reports 18 anaphoras for the Rome 1945 book; the count stays unreconciled until the book is inspected. Compared with the inspected Asmara headings, the 17-anaphora list is consistent with the Keren study's three additions; equivalence of the Asmara Dionysius and Däbrä Zäyt headings with 1945 titles is unverified. Revision documents of 1940 and 1944 are recorded separately (geez-congregatio-orientalis-1940-1944-revision-documents).

source_record.date_basis: Date identifies only the event named in chronology_kind; it is not a period of use, an approval of another book, or a composition date.
source_record.note: The Enciclopedia Cattolica (1951) says Armenian Catholics use the Giafótz (Venice 1686) for the Mass readings and chants. Bibliography 1512-1800 entry 131 describes this Venice lectionary, printed by Gaspar Sahratian and T‘adēos Hamazaspean under Catholicos Eghiazar, with title leaves dated 15 January and 10 September 1686 and an imprint range 1686-1688. source_record.book_label: Ἀκολουθίαι τῶν ἀνωνύμων, 1738
source_record.church_scope: Roman attribution from BnF catalogue; individual Catholic community receipt unestablished
source_record.date: April 1738 printing; Roman imprint attributed by catalogue
source_record.note: The title includes the liturgies of Chrysostom, Basil and the Presanctified gifts; a bounded original Greek witness is acquired in full as offered. Rome and Propaganda Fide are catalogue attributions. Physical completeness, the catalogue 128+100 extent and a direct relationship to the 1754 Euchologion are unresolved. Finisher evidence (2026-10-19): the BnF record cb39303242b transcribes the same Greek title, including the office of Holy Communion, with April of AM 7246 / AD 1738, so identity and date are not disputed. In the offered 202-image witness the first pagination reaches printed p. 91 at provider PP97 (end of the Presanctified Liturgy), followed by an unnumbered dismissal leaf at PP98, whereas BnF gives [2]-128-100 pages; the Sunday Apostle and Gospel readings named on the title were not located in the bounded inspection, so the witness may lack about 36 pages of the first series. Raes (Enciclopedia Cattolica VII, 1951) reports a nine-volume Roman reprint of Arcudius's Anthologion in 1738, and BnF catalogues four further April 1738 Greek office books attributed to Propaganda; whether this volume belongs to such a set is unestablished. Cold review (2026-10-19): the dismissal leaf at PP98 ends with the catchword Ἀπος, which points to Apostle readings that the offered witness does not carry before the second pagination begins at PP99; this strengthens the inference that the Sunday Apostle and Gospel series named on the title is missing from this witness. Charon (Chrysostomika, 1908, printed p. 560) calls this book the Roman edition of the three Liturgies of 1738 and reports that its prototype was the Venice Euchologion of 1727, on which Benedict XIV's commission also based the 1754 Euchologion; that reported common source is recorded without adopting graph ancestry and does not establish direct dependence between 1738 and 1754.

source_record.note: MCI identifies Rome publication as a reform and the Slavonic basis of later English books. Referenced scan URL returns 404; no scan inspected. Additional public route on the UGCC commission page points to Google Drive file 0B4vzPDufLbhuYi1rLUJ6TWNPdms; whole-file request requires Google sign-in. source_record.recension_identity_note: Raes 1947 pp. 85–87 explicitly distinguishes parallel Russian and Ruthenian series, both completed 1942. The 1940/1941 single-liturgy issues precede this complete book; physical format is not a substantive version boundary.
source_record.reception_evidence: The Slovenian translator identifies the 1942 Church Slavonic book as his source and reports the Križevci bishop’s confirmation request (3 June 2022, 92/2022) and dicastery approval (30 November 2022, 152/2022). This documents one approved translation source; original letters and general adoption remain unverified. Regional lane addition (byzantine_regional, 2026-10-19): the IKA report of 27 May 2023 independently names the Rome 1942 Church Slavonic Liturgikon of the Ruthenian recension as the source of the Slovenian translation, issued in three role editions (Služebnik for clergy, Božja liturgija for people and singers, and a notated edition) with episcopal approval no. 14/2023. Separately, the Croatian Chrysostom book printed in February 2018 names a different source, the Rome 1970 Ruthenian-recension Chrysostom printing (PDF/printed p. 4). Neither establishes use of the 1942 book in Croatia generally or in Serbia. Slavic-lane addition (byzantine_slavic, 2026-10-19): Kolupaev (2012, p. 390) examined the 1952 Rome 'Литургикон сиесть служебник' (679 pp.) and states it is a photolithographic reissue of the 1942 book; a Russian Catholic parish library lists the 1952 Liturgikon at 678 pp., Raes's page count for 1942. Slovak scholarship that names the 1952 Liturgikon as binding and as a translation source (Boháč; Mojzes) therefore points to the 1942 text. The UGCC commission's official-books page lists 'Служебник, Рим 1942' as the Church's Church Slavonic Sluzhebnyk. Keleher (p. 23 n. 33) also reports the 1952 Holy See reprint. Kolupaev (p. 388) notes a Tisserant imprimatur dated 17 May 1944 prefacing the 1942 Ruthenian text, a date later than the 1942 imprint; whether the copy he described was a later issue is unresolved. The commission's Google Drive copy of 1942 (file 0B4vzPDufLbhuYi1rLUJ6TWNPdms) still returns a Google sign-in page.

source_record.reception_note: Slipyj, 12 April 1942, reports use of the new Liturgikon at the Lviv seminary and objections among some Stanislaviv priests after initial submission. The letter does not identify a particular printing or prove universal reception. Slavic-lane addition (byzantine_slavic, 2026-10-19): Keleher (2006, pp. 20-21) reports a two-colour Lviv reprint of the new Chrysostom by Metropolitan Andrey in 1942 (5,000 copies, for clergy) and a black-and-white reprint by the Mukachevo eparchy in 1944, probably under Bishop Theodore Romzha. A 1962 Graz photolithographic Chrysostom of 151 pp. held by a Russian Catholic parish library in Saint Petersburg matches Raes's page count for the 1941 small Ruthenian issue; page-count identity is circumstantial. Kolupaev's 1978 small-format Chrysostom reissue repeats the Russian-use (Vulgata) 1941 issue he describes, which includes the troparion 'Господи иже Пресвятаго Твоего Духа' that the Ruthenian recension omits, so it is not a witness of this recension. The Košice eparchy calls the Roman books binding and dates the Ruthena Chrysostom 1941; Boháč names the 1940 Grottaferrata Chrysostom as the Slovak translation source.

Inspection of the final printed folio and following blank leaves supplies a bounded terminal comparison with the separately appended read-Liturgy order in Univ 1733. Slavic-lane addition (byzantine_slavic, 2026-10-19): Zabolotna (NBUV, 2024) reports that the Supraśl part was not issued in every copy of the run, and that NBUV copy Кир.5236п has a Pochaiv [1765] Chrysostom issue (A) and Кир.5548п the Chrysostom leaves of the Pochaiv 1765 Sluzhebnik, each inserted in place of removed originals (Zabolotna 2015), so copy contents vary. Huculak (App. II) separates the 1692 Vilnius edition from the 1695 Supraśl issue with added material and notes that most Catholic Sluzhebniks follow this Zochowski tradition. Keleher (p. 16 n. 8) names the 1683 Grottaferrata Greek Liturgikon as its model and dates the Supraśl issue 1697; both are secondary claims, the latter conflicting with the catalogued 1695.
source_record.relationship_evidence: 1941 circular I §3 identifies the Vilnius 1692 component as a source of rubrics expanded at Univ 1733; this does not date later bound additions or identify a Latin donor edition.
source_record.source_title_status: Original title and imprint inspected
source_record.version_boundary_basis: NBUV copy Кир. 5232 of the 1692–1695 book ends with the Suprasl colophon and blank leaves; the 1733 Univ copy appends a distinct six-page order of the read Liturgy after the corresponding terminal services and its own colophon. The comparison is copy-specific and does not date the first origin of every rubric.
source_record.witness_limit: 1692–1695 is one catalogued imprint interval, not four established versions; exact copy contents and image access require inspection

source_record.church_scope: Melkite Catholic history, or shared Antiochian history before 1724
source_record.date: seventeenth century; compilation, copy and approval dates kept distinct
source_record.date_basis: Compilation, copy and approval dates are disputed; no chronology bounds are given.
source_record.note: Charon reports the Euchologion revision of Meletios Karmé at three dates that he does not reconcile: 1633 for the revision according to a Jerusalem manuscript (Holy Sepulchre ar. 127; printed p. 532); approval of the Vatican copy, Vat. ar. 618, by Patriarch Macarius III in 1643, with its dispatch to Pope Alexander VII for printing at Rome in 1662 (p. 532); and, in the Euchologion section, a recension 'made by Meletios Karmé in 1643' (p. 615), a 357-folio paper quarto. Nassif's 2018 title attaches 1635 to Karmé's Euchologion and calls the Roman project abortive. Charon (pp. 615-623) reports the failed Roman printing. No single coordinate is chosen; compilation, approval, copy and dispatch dates stay distinct.

Printing 1967 versus 1968, press and bilingual-format discrepancies remain unresolved until original title/approval leaves are inspected. Lajme 2023 p. 104 gives decree publication 6 August 1968; the 2018 pastoral p. 30 says adoption decreed 13 October 1968. These reports do not authorize a silently harmonized exact adoption day. source_record.book_label: The Liturgical Prayer Books of the Melkite Greek Catholic Church, four volumes in six parts
source_record.church_scope: Melkite Catholic Church
source_record.date: decree of 1996; exclusive use from Pascha 1997; publication 1997–2000
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies only the event named in date_role; it is not composition, universal adoption or a period of use.
source_record.note: Volume I part 1 September–November and part 2 December–February (Horologion, Paraklitike, Menaion); volume II part 1 February–April and part 2 Holy Week (Triodion); volume III Paschaltide, April–June (Pentecostarion); volume IV June–August (Horologion, Paraklitike, Menaion). In large and small formats. One corpus of complementary parts, not six versions; it is the modern Catholic revision of the Triodion, Pentecostarion and Menaia. The letter states no year per part. The DLI record 44455 (Kitab as-salawat at-taqdisiyah, Jounieh, Paulist press, printed with the permission of Patriarch Maximos V, 'corrected translation on the basis of the Greek original') dates the parts: vol. III (22 March to end of June) 1997; vol. I.1 (1 September to end of November) and I.2 (1 December to end of February) 1998; vol. IV (18 May to end of August) 1999; vol. II.1 (15 January to 25 April) and II.2 (Great Holy Week) 2000. Its date ranges per part differ from the letter's month labels because of the movable cycles. The parts were not acquired.

source_record.church_scope: Greek-rite Catholics served by Roman Greek editions; reception unestablished
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies only the event named in date_role; it is not composition, universal adoption or a period of use.
source_record.note: Raes (Enciclopedia Cattolica VII, 1951; English rendering read whole) reports that from 1873 to 1902 all the Byzantine liturgical books except the Typikon were printed at Rome in 16 volumes, and that the Horologion edition was resumed in 1937. The lane labels five Roman books of 1873-1886 from the DLI catalogue (Euchologion 1873, Horologion 1876, Euangelion 1880, Apostolos 1881, Oktoechos 1886); their membership of the 16 is inferred from the date range only, and the other volumes (for example a Triodion, Pentecostarion, Paraklitike and Menaia, which carry Eucharistic propers) are unidentified. Raes's bibliography cites C. Korolevsky on the Roman edition of the Greek Menaia (Bollettino della Badia greca di Grottaferrata 3, 1949, and 4, 1950) as the next source. No chronology bounds are assigned to a range of printings.

source_record.book_label: Innovations in the Divine Liturgy introduced by Archbishop Angelo of Rossano (elected 1266), as attacked by Theodore of Cursi
source_record.church_scope: Historical Italo-Greek use of the archdiocese of Rossano; no modern Church reception asserted
source_record.date: after 1266 (second half of the thirteenth century); exact year unknown
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies only the event named in date_role; it is not composition, universal adoption or a period of use.
source_record.note: Parenti (section 3, notes 45-46, citing G. Mercati's study of Theodore of Cursi's Antirrhetikos) reports that the archbishop suppressed the three opening antiphons, the litany and prayer for the catechumens and the first series of petitions, simplified the opening invocation of the litanies and the Trisagion, and moved the preparation of the bread and wine to after the Gospel in imitation of the Roman offertory. These are named changes to order and prayers, known from a polemical witness reported in a secondary article; no service book carrying them is identified and their extent and duration are unknown. No chronology bounds are assigned.

source_record.date_basis: Date role: publication-year. It is not composition, universal adoption or a period of use.
source_record.note: Charon says it reprints the 1839 Propaganda Liturgikon in the same typographic disposition and keeps the text of the Roman Euchologion as Benedict XIV required; quarto, 288 pages. No whole-book collation has been made, and no graph ancestry is asserted.

source_record.book_label: Kritsfalusi György, Hungarian translation of the Liturgy of John Chrysostom (manuscript, 1795)
source_record.church_scope: Hungarian Greek Catholics (Mukachevo eparchy era)
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (manuscript-date), not composition, approval of another book or a period of use.
source_record.note: According to the latest, not yet refuted view reported by Dobos 2020 (printed p. 392), the first complete Hungarian translation of the Liturgy of Chrysostom, made by György Kritsfalusi and offered to Bishop András Bacsinszky as a name-day gift in 1795; it was kept in the Uzhhorod episcopal library and published by Sztripszky in 1913. Its closest affinity to the Moscow 1658 Služebnik is a scholarly inference. Open: original manuscript, present location and precise Slavonic exemplar unseen.
source_record.source_title_status: Description in the catalogue; no title inspected

sources.inspection: Reports the latest, not yet refuted view that Kritsfalusi's translation of 1795 is the first complete Hungarian translation; manuscript M–769 copied by István Lupess in 1814 is a variant of it, although a later owner attributed the translation to Mihály Krucsay in 1793; a copy made by Antal Papp at Hajdúdorog in 1854 is also mentioned. The 1882 title page names the book the translation of a nine-member committee of the Mukachevo and Prešov consistories (Hajdúdorog 1879); the book carries no ecclesiastical approval; 1890 added Basil, the Presanctified and priestly office texts. Note 39 records Bishop Dudás's 1954 instruction (ordinance 819 in circular 1954/XIII). Source-affinity arguments point to the Moscow edition of 1658, not to a located exemplar.

source_record.book_label: Calendar reform of the Hajdúdorog eparchy (Gregorian calendar from 24 June 1916)
source_record.church_scope: Hajdúdorog eparchy (with parallel decisions in Mukachevo and Prešov, later reversed or made optional there)
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (effective-date), not composition, approval of another book or a period of use.
source_record.language: Hungarian (circular); applies to the calendar of the liturgical books
source_record.note: Bishop Miklósy's circular 1990/1916 (Körlevelek VI (1916) 25) moved the feasts to the Gregorian calendar from 24 June 1916 after a meeting of 4 May 1916 with the Mukachevo and Prešov bishops, reporting that Pope Benedict XV's approval had been sought; supplementary circular 3150/1916 (Körlevelek XI (1916) 52) made separate provision for the Exaltation of the Cross, St Demetrius and the Protection of the Theotokos (Athanasiana 26, printed pp. 65–68, note 8). Mukachevo restored the Julian calendar on 21 November 1918 and Prešov made it optional; in 1919 some Hajdúdorog parishes had returned to it. source_record.church_scope: Hungarian Greek Catholics (Hajdúdorog eparchy)
source_record.date: 1920 imprint and permission for private use (1235/1920); 1921 distribution and enforcement (circulars 1021 and 1195)
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (printing-approval-implementation-distinguished), not composition, approval of another book or a period of use.
source_record.language: Hungarian, with the canonical parts (anaphoras) of the liturgies also printed in Greek
source_record.note: Revised against the Greek and expanded edition combining the 1882 and 1890 volumes, with the offices of the liturgical day, the Great Canon, dismissals, Sunday propers, calendar and a paschalion for 1921–1960. Its preface states that the canonical parts of the liturgies were printed in Greek as well, so that clergy could celebrate the essential part in the Church's original language until Greek liturgikons could be obtained from Rome (Athanasiana 27 (2008), printed p. 20, quoting the book's 'Emlékezetül', pp. 309–310). Distribution was announced by circular 1195 and the text made binding by circular 1021 of 1921. Open: do not date all public use from the private-use permission alone; book not acquired. Follow-up 2026-10-20: Ivancsó 2007, pp. 69–73, and Ivancsó 2008, pp. 19–25, re-inspected. The approval formula is permission for private use and must remain explicit. Dated circular 1021/1921 directs the revised book’s wording; circular 2351/1949 describes the heavily worn Chrysostom section of 1920 copies and orders a replacement extract. source_record.church_scope: Roman Ruthenian-recension printing; cited as the source of the Croatian Križevci translation of 2018; general reception not established
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (source-publication-as-cited), not composition, approval of another book or a period of use.
source_record.note: The exact source imprint is stated on PDF/printed p. 4 of the Croatian 2018 book. It belongs to the Roman Ruthenian line already held as byz-ruthenian-chrysostom-1940 (Chrysostom issue) and byz-ruthenian-1942 (Liturgikon, same Grottaferrata press); whether it is a later printing of the 1940 issue or differs substantively has not been established, so no new textual state is asserted. Open: coordinate identity with the byzantine_slavic lane before admission; the original 1970 copy was not acquired. Slavic-lane addition (byzantine_slavic, 2026-10-19): No source examined by this lane names a 1970 Ruthenian Chrysostom printing: the UGCC commission's official list gives only the 1942 Church Slavonic Sluzhebnik, Keleher names the 1941 issue and its 1942 Lviv and 1944 Mukachevo reprints, and Kolupaev's survey of Grottaferrata Slavonic books (from copies available to him) omits it. Kolupaev records that 1941 books he presents as printings for Russian-tradition faithful were later repeated: the Presanctified in a 1962 photomechanical reprint made at Graz, Austria, the Vespers in 1968, the Basil in 1969 and the small-format Chrysostom in 1978, with a second 1978 Chrysostom repeating the 1949 edition (2012, pp. 390-391). He also identifies the 1952 Liturgikon as a photolithographic reissue of the 1942 book (p. 390) and records a 1970 photolithographic second edition of an Orthodox St James Liturgy at the same press (p. 392). By analogy with this reissue practice, the 1970 Ruthenian-recension Chrysostom is probably a later printing of the Roman Ruthenian Chrysostom text held as byz-ruthenian-chrysostom-1940 rather than a new textual state. This is an inference, not an inspected finding, and the 1970 printing remains a separate printing witness, not a duplicate. Inspection of its title verso or colophon for a reprint statement remains the deciding check.

source_record.note: One production span, not two editions. Senchenko describes the copy RNB OR VII.3.15 (478 pp.): Josaphat commemorated at the Proskomedia, Creed with Filioque, Pope and King commemorated. source_record.church_scope: Kyivan Uniate metropolia; first Sluzhebnik printed specifically for Catholic Ruthenians (Huculak); later Church mapping requires reception evidence
source_record.date: 1617 (title, Cyrillic numerals); dedication to Lev Sapieha dated Vilnius 1 January 1617 (Kniga Belarusi)
source_record.date_basis: Date identifies the event stated in chronology_kind (publication, approval or attestation as named), not composition or a period of use.
source_record.note: Title leaf inspected: three liturgies and the Presanctified, issued at the expense of Chancellor Lev Sapieha at the Mamonych press. Kniga Belarusi no. 80 gives the collation (29 + 26 unnumbered leaves, pp. 1-473) and contents: Nauka for priests, Proskomedia order, Chrysostom, Basil, Presanctified, blessing of wine, Vespers and Matins orders, dismissals and prayers. Huculak (App. II) calls it the first Sluzhebnik produced for Catholic Ruthenians, without ecclesiastical approval, its Nauka mixing Eastern and Latin practice, and distinguishes it from the Orthodox Holy Spirit Brotherhood Sluzhebnik of the same year (Kniga Belarusi no. 81).
source_record.reception_evidence: Huculak (App. II, p. 386) reports that Bishop Vojna-Orans'kyj of Pinsk (1647-1653), answering Sakowicz's charge that Catholic Ruthenians used Orthodox texts, replied that Catholics were using this Mamonych edition (citing Wawryk). A secondary report of mid-17th-century use in the Pinsk eparchy, not a date of adoption.
source_record.source_title_status: Title leaf inspected at PDF image 1; transcription normalized in label
source_record.version_boundary_basis: Catalogue and repertoire contents: a Nauka (instruction) for priests absent from the Brotherhood edition of 1617 (Huculak, App. II; Kniga Belarusi nos. 80-81).
source_record.witness_limit: Compiled scan includes a modern typescript (image 3), Karataev 1883 entries (images 582-583) and photographs of other pages (584-588).

source_record.note: Kolupaev pp. 390-391: contents Vespers, Compline, Midnight Office, Matins, Liturgy, various orders, menologion, prokeimena and appendices; differs from contemporary Moscow Patriarchate Sluzhebniks by lacking the Izvestie uchitelnoe and naming the feast of All Saints of the Russian land 'в земле русстей'. The parish library catalogue identifies the 1983 book explicitly as Recensione Volgata. Cold review (2026-10-19): the differences Kolupaev lists are against Moscow Patriarchate Sluzhebniks, not against the Roman 1942 or 1953 books. He cites the feast title 'в земле русстей' at p. 47 of the 1983 book (2012, p. 391). Semenenko-Basin and Caprio place the same feast, in the same wording, in the menologion appendix of the 1953 issue at second pagination pp. 47-48 (2021, pp. 382-383). The 1953 issue is the 1942 Vulgata book reissued with appendices, so the 1983 book is probably a reprint of the 1953 issue. Kolupaev's reference list is missing from the delivered PDF, so his reference [12] was not resolved.

source_record.note: Reported reprint of the 1901 ordinary (Coakley citing Delly 1957, p. 170; Sako 2025), printed at the Chaldean patriarchal press in Mosul rather than the Dominican press (Mando; Sako). Macomber cites both Mosul editions at pp. 24–36, but his apparatus records the 1936 printing apart from 1901 at anaphora line 2 (p. 358, a singular reading shared with the oldest witnesses) and line 52 (p. 366, a variant word form). It is a reset printing with at least minor variants, not a facsimile; the extent and nature of those changes are uncollated.

source_record.note: Commission reports Malayalam publication. Pallath 2023 (pp. 25-26, n. 47) and the 1985 decree printed in the 1986 book distinguish two events: the instruction of 20 January 1962 that promulgated the restored Syriac missal printed at Alwaye (the 1960 Taksa, malabar-1960-taksa), and the entry into force on 3 July 1962, by decision of the bishops, of this partly Malayalam book. Complete GPURA scan (142 PDF pages) acquired in research scratch: title leaf (PDF 7) 'സീറോമലബാർ സഭയുടെ കുർബാനക്രമം', Mar Thoma Sleeha Press, Alwaye 1962; imprimatur of seven bishops dated 3 July 1962 (PDF 8); Malayalam order to printed p. 58, then a separately paginated Syriac section bound from the back (sampled PDF 100 and 135). Pallath describes that section as the complete restored Syriac text reproduced; it witnesses that text and is not a new Syriac version unless collation shows change. The approved operative Malayalam order is received Syro-Malabar service-book language under guidance/time-machine.md §11.
source_record.scope_note: The approved operative Malayalam order is received Syro-Malabar service-book language under guidance/time-machine.md §11. The separately paginated Syriac section witnesses the restored Syriac text; its distinctness from the 1960 Taksa is uncollated. source_record.book_label: Vat. sir. 66: pontifical of 1529 with added leaves containing the Liturgy of the Apostles and of Theodore
source_record.church_scope: St Thomas Christians and the Church of the East (shared ancestry); Catholic reception not asserted
source_record.date: 1529 main volume; added Eucharistic leaves undated
source_record.date_basis: No chronology: the Eucharistic layer has no stated date, and the 1529 colophon belongs to another layer.
source_record.note: Assemani (codex LXVI, 128 folios) dates the body to 1529 by its epigraph at f. 94 ff., a pontifical copied at the monastery of Mar Acha near Gazarta from an exemplar of 1276, but excepts the first ten and last twenty-eight leaves, which 'appear' (videntur) to have been added by Joseph, bishop of the Indies, scribe of codices XLVI, LXII and LXV. The anaphoras (Apostles; Theodore at f. 116v) fall within those added leaves. The 1545 date in secondary catalogues is an ownership note at f. 98v. syri.ac also lists a form of consecration of bread and wine rendered from Latin into Syriac (folio not located). Whole BAV digitization acquired in research scratch; folios not read.

Assemani, Vatican Library, is dated 10 April 1763 and states that the missal was collated with the missal printed by Propaganda Fide in 1716 and found to agree with it. Both dates therefore stand on one book: title 1762, approbation 1763. The approbation's statement of agreement fits the 1992 introduction's description of later editions as copies of 1716 apart from trimming; it does not by itself settle the anaphora count, which remains unverified. Canvas 4 of the same copy, the last text page in reading order (catchword REIM.), carries a Garshuni printer's note that names Rome and appears to give a month and year of completion; it has not been transcribed, and its date must be read before the 1762 title and 1763 approbation are treated as the book's complete date evidence.

source_record.note: The Malayalam preface (PDF 3 to 10, printed 1 to 8) says the book contains only the taksas of Mar Yakob and Mar Dionysius bar Salibi. It names Fr. P. T. Geevarghese, M.A. (later Mar Ivanios), among the priests who shared in the translation and revision. By order of Mar Dionysius, Metropolitan of the Malankara diocese, the Syriac scholar Malpan Mattackal Alexandros Kathanar examined the whole translation. source_record.authority: The General Chapter of 1677, under Innocent Le Masson, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse and General of the Order
source_record.citation:
Printed on the engraved title page of the 1679 edition, READ HERE IN THE PAGE
IMAGE on 2026-08-02 and no longer taken from the catalogue: `MISSALE CARTVSIANI
/ Ordinis ex ordinatione Capituli Generalis. / Anno Domini M.D.C.LXXVII. /
Celebrati Sub R.P.D. Innocentio le Masson Priore / Cartusiæ ac totius eiusdem
ordinis Generali` [verified, canvas f5 of ark:/12148/bpt6k9127828m].

THE CATALOGUE'S TYPO IS THE CATALOGUE'S. Gallica's record transcribes the last
words as `totius eiusdem odinis generali`; the engraved plate reads `ordinis`
plainly. The earlier state of this row reproduced `odinis` and flagged it as the
catalogue's own -- that flag was right, and it is now settled at the plate
instead of being a guess about a transcription.

THE ORDINANCE ITSELF IS PRINTED IN THE BOOK, which is better evidence than the
title page and was not previously known to this file. Innocent Le Masson's
prefatory letter at canvas f7, headed `FRATER INNOCENTIVS, Humilis Prior Majoris
Cartusiæ, ac totius Ordinis Cartusiensis Minister Generalis`, recites it and
then quotes its tenor [verified in the page image]: `... ordinationem in Capitulo
Generali anni 1677. edidimus, cujus tenorem hic referre placet. [Quia Missalium
penuria laboramus, ordinamus Missalia ad vsum Ordinis de novo imprimi, ac
propterea monemus Visitatores Provinciarum & Priores Domorum, vt si quid in
ipsis ... addendum` -- the sentence runs onto the following leaf, which was not
fetched, and is therefore cut here at the catchword rather than completed from
guesswork.
source_record.date_note:
TWO YEARS ARE IN PLAY AND THEY ARE NOT COLLAPSED. The chapter met in 1677; the
book was printed in 1679. The station is dated by the PRINTING, 1679, because
that is the state the line reached, and the chapter's year is in `authority` and
in the citation rather than being averaged into the date.

BOTH YEARS ARE NOW VERIFIED ON ONE LEAF, which is the cleanest possible warrant
for keeping them apart: the engraved title plate at canvas f5 carries `Anno
Domini M.D.C.LXXVII.` in its title and `1679` in its imprint at the foot of the
same plate [verified 2026-08-02]. Le Masson's letter at f7 names the chapter
year a third time, as `Capitulo Generali anni 1677`.
source_record.effect: No departure. No unit of this use has been read.
source_record.instrument: The ordinance of the General Chapter of 1677, by which the missal was issued

the engraved title page at canvas f5 and the prior general's prefatory letter at

TWO FACTS ABOUT THE COPY, recorded because neither was in this file. The
digitised exemplar is NOT a BnF copy: the manifest labels it `Bibliothèque
municipale de Grenoble, Vh.258 Rés.`, Gallica hosts it as part of the Grenoble
documentary set `BnGren00`, and a `BIBLIOTHEQUE DE GRENOBLE` stamp is visible on
the title plate itself [verified]. And the imprint, which the catalogue title
does not carry, is engraved at the foot of that plate: `FAVRATII IN SABAVDIA /
Typis Ludouici du Four Sereniss. Ducis Tipographi ordinary Sumptibus maioris
Cartusiæ / 1679`, signed `L. Cossin Sculpsit` -- printed at Fourvoirie in Savoy
at the charge of the Grande Chartreuse.

source_record.dateline: Ex adibus Sacre Congregationis pro Cultu Divino, die 26 martii anni 1970, Feria V in Cena Domini.
source_record.effect: Carries every departure this file records for the Ordinary of the Mass.
source_record.effect_note:
TWO WITNESSES OF ONE DECREE WERE COMPARED HERE, and the comparison is the
opposite of the one the base slice made. Both the 1970 typical edition's text
layer and the 2002 typical edition's print this decree, and both were read here:
the 1970 scan renders `eucharistice`, `Pontice`, `Pontihicis`, `adibus` and
`Sacre`, while the 2002 file renders `eucharisticae`, `Pontifice`, `Pontificis`,
`aedibus` and `Sacrae`. The wording is the same; one delivery loses the ae
ligature and one does not. A diff of the two would report eight changes to a
decree that did not change -- and this time the cleaner reading is the LATER
book, which is the reverse of the usual assumption that older scans are worse.

source_record.effect: No departure in this slice, and the act itself says why not.
source_record.effect_note:
THE ACT LISTS ITS OWN CHANGES AND NONE OF THEM IS IN THIS SLICE, which is a
better reason for an empty station than any this history has had before. Read
here: the description of the offices of acolyte and lector replaces those
treating of the subdeacon at nn. 142-152 of the Institutio generalis; certain
formularies of the ritual and votive Masses are completed with entrance and
communion antiphons; the Masses of the dedication of a church and altar, for
reconciliation, of the Blessed Virgin Mary Mother of the Church and of the Most
Holy Name of Mary are added; and further minor variations are made in titles and
rubrics. This slice carries the Ordinary and Holy Week, and the act touches
neither.

The acquisition audit calls this edition the postconciliar row with no whole
witness located anywhere -- what exists is the Ordo Missae alone, three orders of
magnitude too small. So the emptiness here is partly a real reading of the
decree and partly a bound on the corpus, and both are stated rather than one
being allowed to stand for the other.

Sacred Congregation of Rites, 9 December 1924, operative clause `Vaticana hujus
Missalis editio pro typica habenda est`, with later printings `omnino
conformandae erunt, ita ut in iis nihil immutare fas sit`; dateline `Die 9
Decembris 1924`, subscribed `A. Card. VICO, Ep. Portuen. et S. Rufinae, S. R. C.
Praefectus` and `Alexander Verde, S. R. C. Secretarius` [recorded, as above].
source_record.effect: No departure. No unit of this use has been read.
source_record.effect_note:
THIS STATION IS THE COUNTER-EXAMPLE THAT KEEPS A GENERALISATION HONEST, and it
is why the exempt-uses line is drawn the way it is. The two signatories here --
Cardinal Vico as Prefect and Alexander Verde as Secretary -- are THE SAME TWO MEN
who signed the Roman typical edition's decree of 25 July 1920, in the same
offices, four years apart. So the diocesan uses do not legislate their own
typical editions: Rome does, through the same congregation.

And yet no edge is drawn from the Roman line into this one. One congregation
acting for two rites is a fact about who signs, not a descent of one rite from
the other, and drawing it would make the Braga use look like a branch of the
Roman typical editions. The distinction between an authority and a lineage is
exactly what this file's edges exist to keep.

The decree printed at the head of the edition states what it was made from and

source_record.via_unrepresented_basis:
The same decree says the text was drawn from the other typical edition, that of
1900: `In qua editione, ex altera typica anni 1900 deprompta, illud tantum
innovatum est, quod ex recentibus praescriptionibus liturgicis et ex additionibus
et variationibus, in Breviario typico inductis, consequeretur.` That edition is
not in this corpus and no act promulgating it is cited here, so the edge from the
1634 revision down to 1920 crosses at least one station this record does not
hold. It is drawn as descent, not as succession.

The quotation also bounds the 1920 edition's own reach, and is why this act
carries so few departures: it says that the only thing made new was what followed
from the recent liturgical prescriptions and from the additions and variations
introduced in the typical Breviary.

source_record.act_citation_note:
CORRECTED 2026-08-01. This station carried `act_citation = "not-found"` from the
day it was drawn until the missal acquisition audit read the decree. The
correction, and why the error was made, are both worth keeping.

THE DECREE EXISTS AND HAS NOW BEEN READ, at page 2 of the Vatican typical
edition, in the exact facsimile this repository already had registered. Opening,
with the OCR damage of that text layer reproduced (`rubricanim`, `i960`):

  DECRETUM
  Novo rubricanim corpore, a Summo Pontifice Ioanne XXIII, Motu proprio
  << Rubricarum instructum >> diei 23 iulii anno i960 approbato posteroque die
  a Sacra Rituum Congregatione promulgato, vix fieri non potuit quin eadem
  Sacra Rituum Congregatio novam Missalis romani editionem, ad dictum
  rubricarum codicem plane accommodatam, pararet.

Operative clause: `hinc est quod praesens Vaticana Missalis romani editio uti
<< typica >> declaratur`. Dateline: `Romae, ex aedibus Sacrae Rituum
Congregationis, die 23 iunii 1962`, subscribed `A. M. Card. LARRAONA, S. R. C.
Praefectus` and `Henricus Dante, S. R. C. a secretis`.

So the incipit `Novo rubricarum corpore`, which this file expressly declined to
promote because it was known only from a report, is now read from the book.

WHY THE ERROR WAS MADE, because it is instructive and not careless. This
tracer's corpus is seven Internet Archive OCR text layers, and its 1962 witness
is the BENZIGER printing, which carries a New York imprimatur and not the
Vatican decree. The statement `only three occurrences of DECRETUM in 136,068
lines` was true of that scan. What was false was recording the result in a field
that reads as a claim about the repository -- because the repository held the
decree, in a passage record dated 2026-07-25, six days before this file was
written:
`passage.catholic-church.missale-romanum.vatican-typica-1962.decretum-sacrae-rituum-congregationis-1962`,
states `verified`, locus `front matter, artifact PDF p. 2`.

Two records of one fact, in one tree, never compared. guidance/the-shape.md
section 2. `act_citation` is `cited-externally` rather than `cited-in-corpus`
because the decree stands in the Vatican typical edition, which is not a witness
of this file's corpus; the corpus is unchanged and its own negative result
stands as reported.
source_record.amends:
`attested_in` NAMED ONLY A SUBSTITUTE. The base slice recorded this act as
attested in `benziger-iuxta-typicam-1962` -- a New York printing declared to
conform to the typical edition -- while the act's own `citation` field cited the
Vatican typical edition itself, by artifact id, at page 2 of the CMAA facsimile.
The corroborating witness was named and the controlling one was not, and the
reason it was not is that until this slice registered
`1962-missale-romanum-cmaa` above there was no row to name. That is the same
defect `5420ea2e7` found for the English on 2026-08-01 and `0032bd735` closed for
it on 2026-08-02; the Latin half of it stood until now.

THE BENZIGER IS KEPT AND IS NOT DEMOTED. It attests the same act at one remove,
through the conformity declaration its own row records, and it is the second scan
every corroboration in this repository runs against. What changes is that the
controlling witness now stands first and the record no longer names only the
substitute.

WHY THIS IS AN AMENDMENT HERE AND NOT AN EDIT THERE. The witness row belongs to
this slice: the base slice's `evidence` states in terms that nothing in it has
been read against a page image and that no row of it claims `page-image`, and
that is still true of it. An act in the base naming a witness only this file
carries would be a reference that resolves in the merged history and dangles in
the narrower one, so the reference is made where both ends stand.

NOTHING ELSE ABOUT THE ACT MOVES. `read_from` stays `ocr-only`, because the
decree at page 2 was read in the facsimile's OCR text layer and not off the page
-- the base slice quotes it with the recognition damage intact -- and the day,
the authority, the parentage, the reception basis and the effect are as the base
recorded them.

The merge is drawn because the reception is visible in the book itself, to the
letter, and not inferred from the fact that both acts precede it.

From the 1955 side: section 9 of Maxima redemptionis, fixing the Vigil at
midnight, is reproduced word for word in the witness. The Acta print it at
aas-47-1955 51915-51921 and the book prints it at benziger-iuxta-typicam-1962

front matter, from benziger-iuxta-typicam-1962 1276, with its promulgating decree
at 1235-1272 above it; and its renaming of the Introit is then carried through
into the Palm Sunday propers at 35155.

Where a reception cannot be shown like that, this file draws no merge, and
`act-history check` refuses any act with more than one parent that does not carry
this field.

Pius XI, Inter multiplices gravesque curas, 8 December 1924, printed in the
front matter of the 1924 Missale Bracarense. Dateline as read: `Datum Romae apud
S. Petrum, anno millesimo nongentesimo vicesimo quarto, sexto Idus Decembris, in
festo Immaculatae Conceptionis B. M. Virginis, praecipuae Lusitaniae Patronae,
Pontificatus Nostri anno tertio`, subscribed `A. Card. VICO, Ep. Portuen. et S.
Rufinae` and `Maurus Rigal, Canc. Ap. Tabularii Praefectus` [recorded: the
missal acquisition audit read the whole OCR text layer of the item on
2026-08-01; the item's byte sizes were re-verified here at the metadata API].

source_record.instrument: Bull Inter multiplices gravesque curas
source_record.root_basis:
The record of this line starts here. The Braga use is far older -- a 1558
printing is at the Bibliotheque nationale de France and a 1498 printing is
recorded with no digital facsimile located -- and neither is carried in this run,
so no edge is drawn into this station.

That makes this line unusual and worth noticing: it is the ONLY use line in this
file whose root is an act rather than a printing.

THE 1558 PRINTING WAS REACHED AND READ ON 2026-08-02, and this root is kept
anyway. It is BnF Réserve B-1478, 554 canvases, `Missale juxta usum & ordinem
Almae Bracarensis Ecclesiae Hispaniarum Primatis`, dated 1558 by Gallica's own
record, and its shelfmark is pencilled on the flyleaf at canvas f4 beside the
reference `Weale 198` [verified]. Two things in it are worth a later lane's
attention and NEITHER IS ASSERTED AS AN ACT HERE:

  1.  IT CARRIES WHAT LOOKS LIKE ITS OWN PROMULGATING INSTRUMENT. Canvas f5 is a
      letter headed `BALTHASAR LIMPVS ARCHIEPISCOPVS ET BRACARAE Dominus,
      Hispaniarum Primas: Decano & Capitulo sanctae Bracarensis Ecclesiae, ac
      totius eius prouinciae Clero sanctum exoptat spiritum & salutem in Domino
      sempiternam`, in which Archbishop Baltasar Limpo describes finding the old
      missal `corruptum illud certe vetustate` and having a corrected edition
      made [verified in the page image]. That is an archbishop of Braga ordering
      a Braga missal, four hundred years before the act this line is rooted on.
      IT IS NOT ADDED AS A STATION IN THIS RUN: the letter was read but not
      transcribed whole, it carries no date in the portion read, and adding a
      root below an existing root is a change to the line's shape rather than an
      evidence upgrade. It is the single most promising lead for extending this
      line backwards and it is written down so it is not re-found.

  2.  IT WAS PRINTED AT LYON, NOT AT BRAGA. Gallica's record gives the imprint
      as `Lugduni sumptibus Jo. à Burgundia, bibliopolae regis Lusitanorum,
      1558` [verified] -- at Lyon, at the charge of Jean de Bourgogne, bookseller
      to the King of Portugal. Worth recording because this file carries a
      Lyonnais line as well, and a reader meeting `Lugduni` on a Braga book
      should not take it for a use.

  3.  ONE CAUTION ON THE COPY. Its first printed leaf in the digitisation is the
      Limpo letter; no printed title page was found in the leaves examined, and
      the BnF describes the preliminaries as `[10]` leaves. Whether the title
      leaf is absent from this copy was NOT established, and it is flagged
      rather than resolved.

THE INSTRUMENT WAS NOT READ HERE AND IS BELIEVED TO EXIST. Its title and date
come from two documents that were read at the bytes: Summorum Pontificum names
it `Quattuor Abhinc Annos` beside Ecclesia Dei, and this repository's passage
record for Ecclesia Dei states that the motu proprio's footnote `identifies the
letter Quattuor abhinc annos of 3 October 1984` [recorded:
src/sources/works/john-paul-ii/ecclesia-dei/editions/english-vatican-web-2026-07-25/passages/complete-text.toml].

So the act is named, dated and twice attested by later instruments, and its own
text has not been read. `not-found` is exactly that state, and it is not
`none-claimed`: an instrument is claimed here and is missing, which is a
different thing from a printing for which no instrument is claimed at all.
source_record.act_citation_scope:
ADDED 2026-08-01, and THE SEARCH IT RECORDS FOUND SOMETHING. This is section
7.2's correction happening a second time, caught this time by the rule that
correction produced.

Searched: THIS REPOSITORY'S OWN SOURCE LIBRARY, for `quattuor abhinc annos`,
case-insensitively. Four files answer. Two are inventories, one is the Ecclesia
Dei passage record this note already cites -- and the fourth is
src/sources/works/holy-see/acta-apostolicae-sedis/editions/volume-76-1984/edition.toml,
whose own notes read that the complete 1984 volume `carries the Congregation for
Divine Worship's letter of 3 October 1984 on the use of the Roman Missal of 1962
(Quattuor abhinc annos) at pp. 1088-1089`. That edition has a registered OCR PDF
artifact beneath it.

SO THE INSTRUMENT IS AT NAMED PAGES OF A VOLUME THIS REPOSITORY ALREADY HOLDS,
and `not-found` here means not in the missal corpus this slice reads. The value
is left as it stands because promoting it is a claim that somebody READ the
letter, and nobody has; naming a document and reading it are different acts. The
next lane to touch this station should open pages 1088-1089 of that artifact,
and the station should then become `cited-in-corpus`.

source_record.amends:
QUO PRIMUM IS NO LONGER A ROOT. The base slice drew it as one and said in terms
that it took no position on what preceded it. This slice goes earlier, and the
edge it draws is not a guess: the bull's own opening recites the Tridentine
decree that committed the missal to the Pope. An act that says what it is
executing has drawn its own edge.

The base slice's root basis is kept, not deleted, and is printed as superseded.
It was correct about its own corpus, and a record that quietly stops saying
something it once said is a record a reader cannot check.

Sacred Tridentine Council it fell to us to determine concerning the sacred

dis:  edito  jam,  Deo  ipso  annuente,  ad  populi  eruditionem  Catecbismo,
et  ad  debitas  Deo  persolvendas  laudes  Breviario  castigato
source_record.promulgation_note: Posted at the doors of St Peter's and of the Apostolic Chancery on 29 July 1570, per the subscription printed after the bull in pustet-1862 (OCR lines 276-282).
source_record.root_basis_superseded:
Superseded on 2026-08-01 by the edge above. What it said:

  The earliest act this tracer represents. It is not the beginning of the Roman
  Mass and is not offered as one: what stands before it -- the pre-Tridentine
  curial missal, the 1474 Milan printing, the diocesan uses out of which the
  Tridentine commission worked -- is a live question this tracer takes no
  position on and draws no edge into. A root here means "this record starts
  here", not "nothing preceded it".

Its parenthetical list is still right about the 1474 printing and the diocesan
uses: this slice draws NO edge from any of them into Quo primum either, and the
pre-Tridentine Roman printings it does carry stand on their own line and stop
before 1570. What changed is only that the Tridentine mandate, which the bull
itself cites, is now carried. The quotation supporting the new edge stands at
pustet-1862 OCR lines 158-164, with OCR damage reproduced, including `(..umque`
for `Cumque` and `Catecbismo` for `Catechismo`.

NO INSTRUMENT WAS LOCATED, AND ONE IS BELIEVED TO EXIST. A reprint described as
EMENDED was emended by someone; the 2002 book records the state and not the act.

This station is drawn because omitting it would make a postconciliar recension
silently wrong about 1971 to 1975, and the omission would be invisible: the
missal acquisition audit found this reprint by READING a leaf rather than by
searching, and recorded that a record omitting it `will be silently wrong`.

The value is `not-found` and NOT `none-claimed`, and the difference is the whole
point of having both. A `printed` station claims no act at all; this one says an
act is missing.

The date is `1971` with `date_precision = "year"`, which is what the leaf gives.
No day is invented to make it sort.

This act and the one after it are two halves of one thing and are kept apart
because they are two instruments with two dates and two authorities. The motu
proprio approves the code and orders the Congregation to promulgate it; the
Congregation's decree of the following day promulgates it. Collapsing them would

general Decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites of 23 March 1955 De rubricis
ad simpliciorem formam redigendis ceases to be in force, having been taken up
into this new redaction of the rubrics. An act that says what it supersedes has
drawn its own edge.

constitution orders the rite of the Mass to be revised; it revises nothing

source_record.citation: Francis, Traditionis custodes, 16 July 2021, English text on vatican.va.
source_record.dateline: Given at Rome, at Saint John Lateran, on 16 July 2021, the liturgical Memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, in the ninth year of Our Pontificate. FRANCIS
source_record.effect: No departure in this file, and this station is where the line's whole point becomes visible.
source_record.effect_note:
NOTHING ON THIS LINE MOVES A TEXT, and that is why the line exists separately.
Article 1 declares the postconciliar books the unique expression of the lex
orandi of the Roman Rite; Summorum Pontificum article 1 had called the 1962
edition an extraordinary form of the same rite and said it was never abrogated.
The two are in the record, dated, quoted and NOT reconciled. No merge is drawn
between this line and the Roman one, because a merge asserts a reception and
what these documents show is the opposite.

source_record.citation: Council of Trent, Session XXII, 17 September 1562, Decretum de observandis et evitandis in celebratione missae, in Canones et decreta sacrosancti oecumenici Concilii Tridentini, Leipzig: Tauchnitz, 1887, printed p. 121.
source_record.dateline: SESSIO XXII. QUAE EST SEXTA SUB PIO IV. PONT. MAX., CELEBRATA DIE XVII. SEPTEMBR^S MDLXII
source_record.effect: No departure in this slice. It is the act that makes the Tridentine reform of the missal an answer to something.
source_record.effect_note:
Not a claim that it changed nothing. The decree legislates against abuses --
avarice, irreverence, superstition -- and commits their suppression to the local
ordinaries; it does not itself revise a formulary, and no unit of this slice was
read against it.
source_record.instrument: Decretum de observandis et evitandis in celebratione missae, Session XXII
source_record.locus: 1887-canones-et-decreta-tridentini OCR lines 6287-6355; the session's own heading at 6024-6032
source_record.quotation:
DECRETUM  DE  OBSERVANDIS  ET  EVITANDIS  IN  CE-
LEBR ATIONE  MISSAE.
Quanta  cura  adhibenda  sit,  ut  sacrosanctum  missae  sa-
crificium  omui  religionis  cultu  ac  veneratione  celebretur
[...]
decernit  sancta  synodus,  ut  ordinarii
Iocorum  episcopi  ea  omnia  prohibere  atque  e  medio  tollere
sedulo  curent  ac  teneantur,  quae  vel  avaritia,  idolorum  ser-
vitus,  vel  irreverentia,  quae  ab  impietate  vix  seiuncta  esse
potest,  vel  superstitio,  verae  pietatis  falsa  imitatrix,  induxit.
source_record.quotation_note:
Reproduced with its OCR damage (`omui` for `omni`, `Iocorum` for `locorum`,
`LEBR ATIONE` broken by the scan). The elision spans the decree's opening
argument and a running header.
source_record.root_basis:
The earliest act this file carries, and it is not offered as the beginning of
anything. What stands before it -- the mediaeval Roman curial missal, the
sacramentaries behind that, the uses out of which all of them grew -- is not
represented here and no edge is drawn into this station. A root means the record
starts here.

It is the earliest act rather than the Session XXV decree because it is the
Council's own act about the CELEBRATION OF MASS, and because the reform Quo
primum executed answers the abuses this decree names.

praecipit,  ut  quicquid  ab  illis  prae-
stitum  est  sanctissimo  Romano  Pontifici  exhibeatur,  ut  eius
iudicio  atque  auctoritate  terminetur  et  evulgetur.  Idemque
de  catechismo  a  Patribus,  quibus  illud  uiaudatuni  fuerat,

classification.limitations: Three selected Sanctoral preface comparisons are described by Ward; none is an independent collation of the original altar books. No immediate 1902-to-1981 whole-book succession, complete-book inheritance or first-introduction date is established. Ward distinguishes 1902 abstersit from 1954 abstulit, so the quoted 1954 predecessor must not be silently labelled 1902 wording. The Nativity-of-John preface is shortened/reordered; the Passion-of-John preface is replaced; Sebastian’s replacement is distinct from reuse of older related material as a Common-of-Martyrs collect. The source receipt and corrected transition record article-page image inspection on 2026-10-17.

This is itself a revised printing: its colophon reports restored passages, Gloria/Credo rules, newly added Apollonia and Christian victory Masses, preface notation following Coimbra, and removal of material available in the Manual. These are primary editorial claims, not an independent collation of the complete previous state. Seven Palm blessing prayers plus a preface are directly visible. The physical copy is incomplete; its complete delivered file was acquired.

entries.title: Missale ad usum Sacri Ordinis Cisterciensis (Paris, 1606)

classification.basis: Directly compared complete prayer units show expansion of Confiteor, replacement of Orate and its response, and revised wording and placement of Suscipe sancta Trinitas. The compared Holy Saturday ending and a paired Pentecost-Sunday example add bounded rubrical and appointment changes.
classification.limitations: Text-collated applies to three complete prayer units, their local rubrics, and the Holy Saturday ending on the identified pages. The Holy Saturday quotations are bounded excerpts, not complete service transcriptions. Wider calendar, lectionary, and chant changes have primary-description evidence and have not been exhaustively collated. This is an institutional Cistercian revision relation, not proof that the 1657 typesetter directly copied this particular 1606 edition. All six complete prayer bodies have passed independent image review; one printed accent was corrected. The Holy Saturday rubrics remain a separate bounded review. A further bounded example directly compares 1606 Second Sunday and 1657 First Sunday after Pentecost: numbering and Gospel change, while the identified epistle and chant units are retained. These are descriptive incipits and appointments, not complete literal transcriptions of the propers. This supports one instance of the Monitum claim without verifying all Sundays or comparing every chant against a Roman exemplar.

classification.basis: Deri’s critical comparison identifies omission of the Pentecost-octave Mass and Transfiguration grape blessing in the Paloczi and 1484 comparators relative to the earlier Missale notatum, alongside reduced special-proper and sequence repertories. These named liturgical-content changes support the classification; relocation of preparation material is separately a book-arrangement finding.
classification.limitations: This is an aggregate endpoint change across about 150 years, not a single 1484 promulgation, an immediate parent-child edge, or proof that every omitted item ceased to be celebrated. Preparation placement concerns the book’s arrangement, not the sequence of actions during Mass.
classification.locus: p. XLIII (PDF 53); p. XLV (PDF 55); p. XLI (PDF 51)
classification.scope: Aggregate repertory and named prayer-content differences across the endpoints; not a single 1484 promulgation or immediate revision from the early witness. Preparation placement is not evidence of altered ritual order.

source_record.date: Composite: ff. 1–18 sacramentary copied in the first half of the eighth century; ff. 19–99 sacramentary copied in the second half (ELMSS 104/105)
source_record.qualification: Uncertain place of origin. 1958 critical edition is a modern presentation of the witness, not a new liturgical version. ELMSS 104/105 separate two sacramentaries with different copy dates (701–750 and 751–800); ff. 100–106 (Decretum Gelasianum) are not a third sacramentary. The former single 675–725 coordinate does not fit the composite. The layers are proposed as latin-early-elmss-104 and latin-early-elmss-105, which carry the copying coordinates; this composite row has none, because the two copyings are distinct events and the date at which the parts were bound together is not established.

source_record.date: Ninth century; IRHT 846–855 conflicts with Westwell's 860s before 867
source_record.qualification: Named royal intercession at f. 48r and chapel inventories ff. 116v, 124v support a royal association, not a cathedral-wide Monza Eucharistic recension. Westwell's northeastern-French manufacture and Cysoing/Eberhard transfer are qualified arguments; IRHT origin Monza is not silently adopted as manufacture. No historical-parentage or local adoption edge is asserted.
source_record.source_locus: Westwell (2024) introduction pp. 6–7 and Appendix 2 pp. 419–425: 125 leaves; Preface/Canon ff. 1v–5v, Gregorian body ff. 5v–115v; Hoffmann (2005) p. 71 corrects 89 to 98 (Bischoff 2898); IRHT 614133 gives 98.
source_record.title: Monza treasury Sacramentary of Berengar, 98 (89 in some scholarship)

sources.inspection: Complete PDF; title, key to manuscripts, ch. 1 Gelasian/Gregorian sections, ch. 3 selected supplement passages and manuscript bibliography. Witnesses local compilation and supplement diversity; disputed archetypes must not become universal linear reforms. Additional bounded Monza inspection on 2026-10-20: Whole Arthur Westwell, The Carolingian Sacramentaries of Saint-Amand (2024), 514 PDF pages acquired. Introduction pp. 6–7, Appendix 2 pp. 419–425 (PDF pp. 445–451), and related discussion read; Appendix 2 p. 419 visually inspected. Distinguishes treasury Berengar (called Ms.89) from F.1/101. Catalogues Mass components and later additions by folio. The date, northeastern-French manufacture and possible Cysoing/Eberhard relationship remain the author's argument, not an established Monza local-use or donor-book edge. Additional bounded Ravenna-fragment inspection on 2026-10-20: Whole book PDF acquired from institutional repository; title/rights page, p. 42, note 121 / PDF p. 68, 56 note 180, 58-62 and note 201 inspected. Discusses Montecassino 271 as a mass-prayer/reading book, the single Stockholm-Wroclaw codex, and the evidential limits of Gamber's Ravenna archetype hypothesis. LIMIT: Critical discussion does not independently date or locate the fragment scriptoria. No Ravenna archetype is promoted to a surviving book or historical stage. PDF figures carry separate rights.
sources.label: Arthur Westwell, The Carolingian Sacramentaries of Saint-Amand (2024)

source_record.date: 680–691 per ELMSS 648, USUARIUM and the IA catalogue note (written, or copied from a book written, under Abbot Cronan of Bangor, County Down)
source_record.qualification: One Irish manuscript from Bangor, County Down. USUARIUM records it twice (book 1025, origin 'Bangor, County Down'; book 6091, origin 'Bangor', whose own remark places the monastery in Down) and the Gamber index has matching rows 150 and 1968:0150; merged here as one manuscript identity, not a Welsh Bangor book. Predominantly an Office book (canticles, hymns, collects and anthems for the hours). Its Eucharistic material is limited to identifiable items: the communion hymn 'Hymnus quando communicant sacerdotes', 'Ad pacem celebrandam', collects/anthems 'Ad communionem', and the anthems Warren numbers [109]–[115] and calls Eucharistic. It contains no Mass order or sacramentary. Folio loci of the Eucharistic items not checked against the facsimile (HBS 4); identification rests on Warren's 1895 contents and introduction in uncorrected OCR. Edition date: USUARIUM 1025 and IA metadata give 1893 for part II, but the part II OCR title block reads 1895; part I is catalogued as 1893 (IA metadata, title page not checked). ELMSS 648 (CLA 3.311, fetched by the cold reviewer on 2026-10-19) dates the book VII ex (680–691), written at Bangor during the abbacy recorded in the hymn on its last page; ELMSS names that abbot Colman, whereas USUARIUM and the edition tradition name Cronan. Andrzej Suski, Łacińskie rękopisy liturgiczne zachowane jako palimpsesty. Katalog (2022)

source_record.qualification: This undertext is the libellus of Gallican Masses edited by Mone (1850) and known as the Mone Masses: Suski 2022, entry [47], identifies these Aug. 253 folios as a libellus missarum gallicanus (Missae Mone), VII (630–640), France (Burgundy), CLLA 203, CLA VIII 1102, which is ELMSS 1569. Suski's narrower 630–640 is attributed; the coordinate follows ELMSS VII. Distinct from the other Aug. 253 undertexts (ELMSS 1567, 1568, 1570). The number of Masses and their relation to other Gallican books are not collated here; the retained Mone 1850 scan has no usable text layer. Host BLB PDF is the 372-page Aug. 253 codex, not a complete missal; this candidate links only its ELMSS 1569 bounded folio segment. No legible undertext transcription or textual collation is claimed.

source_record.qualification: ELMSS 715: a Gregorian sacramentary written doubtless in Italy in a neat later-type uncial, erased and rewritten with Gregory's Dialogi in the Beneventan zone in the eleventh century. A Gregorian book copied around 700 witnesses the Gregorian tradition before the Hadrianum reached Francia; its exact Mass components and its relation to the Hadrianum and to the pre-Hadrianic witnesses (Trent 1590, the Clm 6333 layers) are unresolved. Kept in this lane because the packet's use latin-early-use-roman-sacramentary-fragments-italy names it as a Roman-type fragment and the Italian lane's files in this pass hold no record for it. Copying date only.

source_record.qualification: Sedda Anthony Mass scheme III (Haymonian). A missal headed 'Ordo missalis fratrum Minorum secundum consuetudinem Romane Curie': Roman script, northern-French decoration, and a fourteenth-century note tying it to the chapter of St Peter's. The calendar is of Minorite use, but Sedda leaves open whether it served a St Peter's canon conforming to Minorite use under Nicholas III. The added Corpus Christi Mass (ff. 2v–3v) is a later layer. source_record.qualification: Rusca Lanzada L-77 (printed p. 49) catalogues a Rome Vatican 1635 'Secunda editio' with saints' proper Masses set out at length; its copy is incomplete after p. 4 of the final sequence. Asachiana 19 (2023), printed pp. 15-16, photographs another Rome Vatican 1635 title leaf and describes a defective/composite copy, but its stated 698-page complete extent does not reconcile with its section breakdown. Whether these are the same or different settings/issues, or whether either changes the 1634 text substantively, is unverified. Bibliographic witness lead only; no new stage. SBN adds Rome Vatican bibliographic records for explicitly Secunda editio (UM1E041839: [40],444,LXXVI), Tertia editio (PBEE017510: [40],448,LXXVI,[4]), and a larger setting without a transcribed edition label (UM1E008100: catalogue displays [56!,572,XCVII,[3! pages). Preserve them as distinct setting/issue leads until original title and collation verify identity. No new recension/station or 1634/1635 parentage.

evidence.claim: Mandate dated 3 October 1486; corrected books and order-wide uniformity are prescribed.

stages.label: 1487 corrected Cistercian missal
stages.limitations: Already a corrected printed state, not a proxy for every medieval Cistercian manuscript. Retained source images and bounded readings do not provide a checked canonical text transcription.
stages.reception: The mandate directs houses to acquire and use corrected books; no house-by-house reception chronology has been established.
stages.scope: Printed order missal prepared under the 1486 commission for uniform corrected liturgical books.
stages.summary: The opening mandate of Johannes abbot of Cîteaux orders corrected missals, breviaries and psalters under general-chapter authority and directs houses to acquire and conform their books. The colophon dates this printing to 4 September 1487. Its Memento lacks two clauses found in 1606, while both Canon openings retain the king among named intercessions.
stages.witness_label: Missale Cisterciense, Strasbourg, Johann Grüninger, 1487; BSB 2 Inc.c.a. 1921, bsb 00044164; USUARIUM 423

evidence.claim: Explicit reforms of the 1601 and 1605 chapters; full conformity in the Canon, limited conformity elsewhere.
Three bounded prayer units directly transcribed from page images.

Complete bounded offertory constituent independently collated, including all intervening rubrics and response cues. The literal binding and extent census remain separate from partial whole-book text coverage.

stages.label: 1606 Romanizing Cistercian missal
stages.limitations: This is already a revised state, not a proxy for all medieval Cistercian practice. The exact 1606 witness has now been split from the earlier broad printed-witness cluster. No claim that every decree of 1601 or 1605 was fully received locally.
stages.reception: The book identifies itself as for the Cistercian Order and invokes chapter authority; no monastery-by-monastery reception census has been made.
stages.scope: Printed order missal implementing Roman conformity in the Canon while retaining Cistercian usages elsewhere.
stages.summary: The 1606 Annotanda attributes full Roman conformity in the Canon to the 1601 and 1605 general chapters, and conformity elsewhere only as proper Cistercian use allows. The printed Ordinary still has a short Confiteor, a combined Suscipe Trinitas offering, and Orate/Dominus sit response.
stages.witness_label: Missale ad usum Sacri Ordinis Cisterciensis, Paris, Dionysia Cavellat, 1606; BSB 2 Liturg. 205 a

evidence.claim: The general chapter held in May 1651 authorized three learned men to correct the books; the 1655 mandate extends the printing privilege.
Primary description of the new revision; retained graduals prevent complete Roman imitation.
Three complete paired prayers and their position in the offertory read from images.

Complete bounded offertory constituent independently collated, including all intervening rubrics and response cues. The literal binding and extent census remain separate from partial whole-book text coverage.

stages.label: 1657 further Roman correction
stages.limitations: The 1651 commission, 1655 mandate, and 1657 publication are distinct dates. The inspected 1655 instrument is not a universal effective-date decree. The Monitum historical catalogue of earlier defects must not all be assigned specifically to 1606.
stages.reception: The Cistercian superior authorizes the edition and printing monopoly; this is evidence of intended order use, not uniform local implementation.
stages.scope: Printed Cistercian missal following the 1651 commission; a substantially Romanized Ordinary while retaining order-specific material.
stages.summary: The Ordinary enlarges the Confiteor with named saints including Bernard and triple culpa; replaces the old Orate and response; prints separate host and chalice offerings and a revised Suscipe Trinitas after Lavabo. The Monitum reports reordered Pentecost-to-Advent Sunday Masses and Roman rubrics, but expressly retains differences in the graduals.
stages.witness_label: Missale Cisterciense iuxta Romani recogniti correctionem, Paris, Sebastianus and Gabriel Cramoisy, 1657; Krzeszów copy, FIDES 3755

No authorization, adoption day or post-1570 continuation is inferred from the printed witness.

The apparent discrepancy with printer chronology makes 1519 the most likely production year in the checked bibliographic study. This is a book-state attestation, not a claim that a reform took effect in either year.
stages.witness_label: BNP RES.155 A printed Évora missal

evidence.claim: Original folios identify bounded Maundy Thursday prayer/rubric material; the colophon dates the Dupré and Huym printing to 22 September 1481.
